title: DAW Fundamentals & Signal Flow
skill: Navigate a DAW and trace signal flow from a sound source through effects to the master output.
content:
The DAW is a mixing console you can see

Every digital audio workstation (Ableton Live, FL Studio, Logic, Bitwig, Studio One) is the same idea wearing different paint: tracks hold sound sources, those sources route through a chain of effects, every track feeds a channel on a virtual mixer, and the mixer sums down to a single stereo master output that becomes your exported file. If you understand that path, switching DAWs is a weekend, not a career.

The three track types

  • Audio tracks play recorded samples and stems — your kick one-shots, vocal chops, field recordings.
  • MIDI / instrument tracks hold note data (pitch, velocity, length) that triggers a virtual instrument. MIDI is not sound; it is instructions. The instrument turns instructions into audio.
  • Return / send / bus tracks receive audio from other tracks so several channels can share one reverb or one compressor.

Signal flow, in order

Trace it once and it sticks. Sound is generated at the top of a channel and flows downward through every device before reaching the fader:

  1. Source — sample playback or a synth/sampler instrument generates audio.
  2. Insert effects — devices in series, top to bottom: EQ, compressor, saturation, delay. Order matters; EQ-then-compress sounds different from compress-then-EQ.
  3. Sends — a copy of the signal is tapped off (pre- or post-fader) to a return track.
  4. Channel fader & pan — final level and stereo position for that track.
  5. Routing — the channel feeds a group bus or goes straight to the master.
  6. Master bus — all channels sum here; this is where your master chain and limiter live.
Gain staging starts now. Aim for each track to peak around -12 to -6 dBFS and keep the master peaking below -6 dBFS while you produce. Leaving headroom means your mix and master engineers (future you) have room to work. A master pinned at 0 dBFS the whole project is already clipped.

Inserts vs sends — the distinction that confuses everyone

TypeSignalUse it for
InsertWhole signal passes through the deviceEQ, compression, distortion — things that should affect the entire sound
Send (return)A copy is sent; you blend wet back inReverb, delay — shared ambience across many tracks, mixed by taste

Use one reverb on a return and send your snare, claps and synth to it, and they all sit in the same room — cohesive and CPU-cheap. Put a separate reverb insert on every track and you get a muddy hall of mirrors and a melted laptop.

Latency, buffer and freezing

The audio buffer (e.g. 128, 256, 512 samples) trades latency for stability. Use a small buffer (128) while playing synths so they respond fast; raise it (512+) while mixing so plugins don't crackle. When a track is finished and CPU-hungry, freeze or bounce it to audio to reclaim processing.

Tempo, grid and the transport

Set your project tempo before you do anything — most club music lives between 120 and 130 BPM for house/techno, 140 for dubstep/trance, 170+ for drum & bass. The grid (bars and beats, snapped to 1/16 by default) is the canvas. Learn the transport shortcuts in your DAW: play/stop, loop, metronome, and quantize. These are the keys you'll press ten thousand times.

Save like a professional. Save versions (v1, v2, v3) and enable autosave. DAWs crash. A track named final_FINAL_v9 that exists beats a perfect arrangement that vanished.
exercise: Build a one-channel signal chain and trace it by ear. Create one audio track with a drum loop, add an EQ then a compressor as inserts, send it to a return track with a reverb, then watch the loop's level on the channel fader and the master meter. Mute and unmute each device to hear exactly what each stage in the flow does.

tracks.title: Strings of Life
tracks.why: A track built from simple looped layers — load and study how few elements stack into a full arrangement.

tracks.title: Gypsy Woman

title: Drum Programming, Groove & Swing
skill: Program a drum pattern with groove and swing that grooves the way a beatmatched mix taught you to feel time.
content:
From counting beats to making them

You already feel the bar from beatmatching — the kick on every beat, the 32-count phrase. Programming drums is that same internal clock, now drawn onto a grid. A 4/4 bar splits into 16 steps (four 1/16 notes per beat). House and techno live and die on those 16 steps.

The skeleton of a four-on-the-floor groove

  • Kick on steps 1, 5, 9, 13 — every downbeat. This is the heartbeat.
  • Clap or snare on steps 5 and 13 — the backbeat (beats 2 and 4). This is what makes heads nod.
  • Closed hi-hat on the offbeats, steps 3, 7, 11, 15, or on every 1/8 for drive.
  • Open hi-hat on the offbeat (steps 3/7/11/15) for the classic house "tss" that pulls you forward.
ElementSteps (1-16)Role
Kick1 5 9 13Pulse / energy
Clap5 13Backbeat
Closed hat3 7 11 15Offbeat lift
Open hat3 7 11 15Forward motion

Velocity: the difference between a drum machine and a drummer

A pattern where every hit is the same loudness sounds like a typewriter. Vary velocity. Make the downbeat hats slightly quieter than the offbeats; let ghost notes sit at velocity 40-60 while accents hit 100-120. Human players accent and relax constantly — your velocity lane is where you fake that.

Swing and groove

Swing delays every other 1/16 step, pushing it late so the rhythm shuffles instead of marching. Most DAWs express this as a percentage:

  • 50% = no swing, dead straight (techno often lives here).
  • 54-58% = subtle groove, the sweet spot for most house.
  • 62-66% = heavy shuffle, garage and soulful house territory.

Ableton's groove pool and MPC swing templates (the famous 16-level MPC60 swing) let you stamp a feel onto programmed parts. Apply swing mainly to hats and percussion; keep the kick dead-on so the floor stays anchored.

Quantize is a tool, not a religion. Snapping everything to 100% strength kills the feel. Try quantize strength at 70-90% so notes move toward the grid but keep some of your hand's natural push and pull. Perfectly on-grid is not the same as in-the-pocket.

Layering the kick

One kick sample rarely does it all. Producers layer a sub kick (low body, 50-90 Hz) with a punch/click layer (the transient attack, 1-5 kHz). High-pass the click layer so it doesn't fight the sub, and keep both kicks in mono. We'll lock this against the bassline next lesson.

Percussion and the second loop

Once the core loop grooves, add a layer of texture: shakers, congas, rimshots, a ride. Pan them slightly off-center (10-30%) to open the stereo field — but keep kick, snare and sub centered. Program a 2-bar or 4-bar pattern, not just 1 bar, and add a small variation (an extra hat, a dropped clap) every 4th or 8th bar so the loop breathes and never feels copy-pasted.

Reference against a record you love. Load a track whose drums you admire on a muted channel, then A/B your loop against it for groove and balance. Your ears recalibrate fast when the bar is sitting right next to you.
exercise: Program a 2-bar house loop and groove it. Place the kick on every downbeat, claps on 2 and 4, and offbeat open hats, then vary the velocities so accents and ghost notes differ. Sweep the swing from 50% to 62% while it loops and stop where it feels best, then add one variation in the second bar.

tracks.title: Can You Feel It
tracks.why: A masterclass in groove from minimal drums — study the swing and the space between hits.

tracks.title: Percolator
tracks.why: Stripped-back percussion that shows how velocity and offbeat hats create relentless drive.

title: Basslines & the Kick/Bass Relationship (Sidechain)
skill: Write a bassline that locks with the kick using sidechain so the low end is tight and punchy.
content:
The most important relationship in dance music

The kick and the bass share the same real estate — the bottom 200 Hz of the spectrum. If they fight, your low end turns to mud and the track loses punch on a club system. The whole game is making them take turns: kick punches, then bass fills the gap. Sidechain compression is how you enforce that.

Writing a bassline that locks

  • Keep it in the same key as your chords/melody, usually rooting on the track's tonic.
  • Start off the kick: if the kick is on steps 1, 5, 9, 13, put bass notes on the offbeats (steps 3, 7, 11, 15) so they physically don't collide — the classic "jacking" house bass.
  • Keep the sub content (below ~100 Hz) in mono. Stereo bass disappears on big mono club subs and causes phase problems.
  • Resist big movement in the lowest octave. Let the sub stay simple; add melodic interest with a higher mid-bass layer if you want movement.

Sidechain compression, step by step

Put a compressor on the bass channel and feed the kick into its sidechain input (in Ableton, set the compressor's sidechain source to the kick track). Now every kick hit ducks the bass:

ParameterStarting valueWhat it does
Ratio4:1 to 8:1How hard the bass ducks
Attack0.1-1 ms (fast)Duck immediately when kick hits
Release80-150 msHow fast bass returns — tune to tempo
ThresholdSet for 4-8 dB gain reductionThe pumping depth

The release is the musical control. Too short and you barely hear the duck; too long and the bass never recovers before the next kick, so it stays quiet and weak. Watch the gain-reduction meter pump back to zero just as the next kick arrives.

Volume-shaper sidechain is more reliable. A dedicated ducking plugin (LFOTool, Volume Shaper, Kickstart) lets you draw the exact ducking curve, locked to tempo, independent of the kick's dynamics. For a clean, consistent pump this beats a real compressor because it isn't fooled by varying kick levels.

EQ the kick and bass to share the floor

Sidechain handles the time domain; EQ handles the frequency domain. Decide who owns the very bottom:

  • Find the kick's fundamental (often 50-60 Hz) and gently dip the bass there, or vice versa.
  • High-pass everything that isn't kick or bass above 100-150 Hz to clear the basement.
  • Use a spectrum analyzer on the master — you should see the kick and bass alternating, not piling up.

Mono-check the low end

Insert a utility/mono button or a mono meter and collapse the mix to mono. The bass should stay loud and solid. If it thins out or vanishes, you have stereo content too low; narrow it. Sound systems in clubs are mono in the subs — this check is non-negotiable.

Reference loud, then turn down. Big low end feels great loud and disappears quiet. Mix your kick/bass relationship at a moderate volume and check it both quiet and on headphones. If it punches at low volume, it will destroy on a rig.
exercise: Write a mono bassline on the offbeats and sidechain it to your kick. Set a fast attack, 6 dB of gain reduction, and tune the release so the bass swells back exactly before each kick lands. Collapse the mix to mono and confirm the low end stays solid, then A/B with the sidechain off to hear how much tighter it gets.

tracks.title: Music Sounds Better with You
tracks.why: Iconic sidechain pump — the whole track breathes around the kick, a perfect ducking reference.

tracks.title: Da Funk
tracks.why: A fat, locked kick-and-bass groove that shows low-end discipline in a club banger.

title: Chords, Melody & Theory to Write Hooks
skill: Write a memorable hook using just enough music theory to build chords and melodies that fit in key.
content:
You need less theory than you think

You don't need a conservatory degree to write a hook. You need a key, a scale, a handful of chords, and a melody that lives inside them. Master a small amount and you'll write parts that fit together every time instead of guessing.

Pick a key and a scale

A scale is just the seven notes that sound "right" together. Start in A minor — its notes are all the white keys (A B C D E F G), so you can't play a wrong note. Minor keys sound moody and serious (most house and techno); major sounds bright and happy. Whatever key you choose, set it in your DAW's scale/key tool so off-key notes get greyed out or snapped in.

Building chords by stacking thirds

A triad is three notes: a root, skip one, the next, skip one, the next. In A minor: A-C-E is Am, D-F-A is Dm, E-G-B is Em. Each note of the scale gets its own chord, and they fall into a fixed pattern of major and minor:

Scale degreeChord in A minorQuality
iAmminor (home)
IIICmajor (uplift)
ivDmminor (tension)
v / VEm / Eminor / major (pull home)
VIFmajor (emotional)
VIIGmajor (lift)

Progressions that always work

A progression is just an order of chords, usually 4 or 8 bars looped. Reliable starting points in A minor:

  • i - VI - III - VII (Am - F - C - G) — the most-used emotional loop in dance music.
  • i - VII - VI - VII (Am - G - F - G) — driving and hypnotic.
  • i - iv - VI - V (Am - Dm - F - E) — classic and a little dramatic.
Voice your chords low and wide. Play the same triad an octave higher or invert it (move the bottom note up an octave) to keep movement smooth. Inversions stop the bass jumping around and make pads sound professional. Add the 7th (e.g. Am7 = A-C-E-G) for that deep-house jazzy color.

Writing the melody / hook

The melody is the part people hum on the way home. Rules of thumb:

  1. Use notes from the same scale — they'll fit your chords automatically.
  2. Land on chord tones (the notes of the current chord) on strong beats; passing notes can sit between.
  3. Less is more. A hook is often 3-5 notes with rhythm and space. Repetition is what makes it memorable — repeat the motif, then change the ending.
  4. Give it a shape: rise then fall, or a question-and-answer between two phrases.

Tension and release

The reason a drop hits is that the breakdown built tension. Chords do this too: ending a phrase on the V or VII chord leaves the ear hungry, and resolving back to the i (home) satisfies it. Use that — hold the listener on a non-home chord through a build, then slam home on the drop.

Steal the framework, not the notes. Find a hook you love, work out its progression and contour in your DAW, then write something new on the same skeleton. That's how every producer learned — and it keeps you legal.
exercise: Write a 4-chord loop and a hook over it in A minor. Use the progression Am - F - C - G as held chords, then write a 4-5 note melody using only white keys that lands on chord tones on the downbeats. Repeat the motif twice and change its last two notes the second time so it feels like a question and an answer.

tracks.title: Children
tracks.why: A piano hook built from simple in-key chords and a singable melody — textbook tension and release.

tracks.title: Strobe
tracks.why: Study how a small chord progression and a minimal melodic motif carry an entire track.

title: Sound Design, Synthesis & Sampling
skill: Design original sounds with synthesis and sampling to give your track its own sonic identity.
content:
Why design your own sounds

Presets are everyone's. The fastest way to sound generic is to use the factory patch untouched; the fastest way to sound like you is to build and mangle your own. You have two raw materials: synthesis (generating sound from oscillators) and sampling (capturing and reshaping recorded sound).

Subtractive synthesis — the core you must know

Nearly every synth (Serum, Sylenth, Massive, Diva, your DAW's stock synth) is built on the same signal path. Learn it once:

StageWhat it doesKey controls
OscillatorGenerates the raw toneWaveform (saw, square, sine, noise), pitch, detune
FilterRemoves frequencies to shape timbreCutoff, resonance, type (low/high/band-pass)
Amp envelopeShapes volume over timeAttack, Decay, Sustain, Release (ADSR)
LFOModulates a parameter rhythmicallyRate (sync to tempo), depth, destination
EffectsColor and spaceDrive, chorus, reverb, delay

The building blocks of timbre

  • Saw = bright and buzzy, the workhorse for leads and basses.
  • Square = hollow and woody, great for plucks and chip sounds.
  • Sine = pure, no harmonics — your sub bass and bell tones.
  • Noise = the raw material for risers, snares and percussion.

Detune two or three saw oscillators a few cents apart for a thick supersaw lead. The filter cutoff with an envelope on it gives you the classic "wow" pluck — fast attack, the filter opens then closes. An LFO synced to 1/8 on the cutoff gives a wobble; on pitch it gives vibrato.

ADSR is where character lives. A short attack + short decay + zero sustain = a pluck. Slow attack + full sustain = a pad. Same oscillator, two completely different instruments. Spend real time on envelopes; they shape feel more than any preset name.

Sampling: capture, chop, mangle

A sampler maps an audio clip across the keyboard so you can play it melodically. Workflow:

  1. Source a sound — a vocal, a vinyl break, a field recording, a single hit. Royalty-free packs and your own recordings keep you clear of copyright.
  2. Chop it to transients or slice into a kit across keys.
  3. Process: pitch it down for a darker, grittier feel; reverse it; time-stretch it; run it through a bit-crusher or filter.
  4. Resample — bounce the result to audio and process it again. Layering generations of processing is how unique textures are born.

Layering for identity

One sound is rarely enough. A signature lead might be a synth saw layered with a pitched vocal sample and a noise transient. Tuck a quiet detuned octave under a bass. Glue layers together with shared reverb on a send and a touch of saturation so they read as one instrument, not three.

Save your patches and chains as you go. When you stumble onto a sound you love, save it as a preset and a one-shot bounce immediately. That captured sound becomes part of your personal palette — and the seed of a sample pack you can sell later.

Make it move

Static sounds get boring over four minutes. Automate the filter cutoff opening across a build, modulate the LFO depth, or slowly detune. Movement keeps a sound alive and gives the arrangement somewhere to go.
exercise: Build one signature lead from scratch. Start with two detuned saw oscillators, shape a pluck with a fast filter-envelope (short attack and decay, low sustain), then add an LFO on the cutoff synced to 1/8. Resample the result, pitch the bounce down an octave, and layer it back under the original to create a sound that's uniquely yours.

tracks.title: Windowlicker
tracks.why: Extreme synthesis and sample mangling — a study in how processed sounds become an identity.

tracks.title: Gabriel
tracks.why: Warm, characterful sampled and synthesized textures that define the track's signature vibe.

title: Arranging a DJ-Friendly Track
skill: Arrange a track with intro, build, drop, breakdown and outro structured for easy DJ mixing.
content:
Arrangement is your loop, told as a story

You've got a great 8-bar loop. Arrangement is deciding when elements enter and leave so it becomes a 6-minute journey — and, crucially for a club record, so another DJ can mix in and out of it without a fight. Everything happens in phrases: groups of 8, 16 or 32 bars. DJs count in 32s; build your structure on the same grid and your track will mix like a dream.

The DJ-friendly skeleton

SectionTypical lengthWhat's playing
Intro16-32 barsDrums + minimal elements, kept simple for mixing in
Build 116 barsAdd bass, percussion, a hint of the lead
Breakdown16-32 barsDrums drop out, chords/vocal/melody take over, tension rises
Build / riser8-16 barsSnare roll, riser, filter sweep, drums re-enter
Drop / main32 barsFull energy — every element, the payoff
Breakdown 216 barsPull back, vary, reset for the second drop
Drop 232 barsFull energy again, often the biggest
Outro16-32 barsStrip back to drums for mixing out

The two non-negotiables for DJs

  1. A long, beat-driven intro — at least 16 bars of just drums (and maybe a percussion loop) with no melody. This is the runway a DJ blends over. A track that opens with a full vocal and melody is murder to mix.
  2. A matching outro — strip back to drums at the end so the next track can come in cleanly. Intro and outro are the handles your record is grabbed by.
Build on 8s, change on 16s and 32s. Make significant changes land on phrase boundaries (every 8, 16 or 32 bars). DJs feel these boundaries from beatmatching; if your changes happen off-grid, the track feels lumpy and won't mix cleanly.

Tension and release across the arrangement

The drop only hits because the breakdown removed the kick and bass and made you crave them. Use the tools you know from DJing — filter sweeps, risers, a snare roll accelerating from 1/8 to 1/16 to 1/32, an uplifter, a reverse cymbal, silence right before the drop (a beat of dead air makes the drop feel twice as big). The classic move: cut everything for one beat, then slam the full drop on the downbeat.

Variation so it never gets boring

Identical 32-bar sections feel like a loop, not a song. Each time a section returns, change something: add a counter-melody, drop the hats for 4 bars, throw in a vocal stab, automate the reverb wider. Small differences keep the ear engaged over four to six minutes.

Transitions between sections

Don't hard-cut between sections cold. Use a crash on the downbeat of a new section, an impact/boom, or a fill in the bar before. A 1-bar drum fill or a reverse-reverb swell signposts "something is about to change" and makes the arrangement feel composed rather than assembled.

Reference a club track's structure. Drop a record from your target genre into your DAW, look at where its sections start in bars, and copy the timing skeleton. You'll discover how disciplined the phrase lengths really are.
exercise: Arrange your loop into a full DJ-friendly track. Lay out a 16-bar drums-only intro, a 16-bar breakdown that drops the kick and bass, a build with a snare roll and riser, then a 32-bar full drop, and finish with a drums-only outro. Put every major change on an 8- or 16-bar boundary and add one beat of silence right before the drop.

tracks.title: Opus
tracks.why: A long, patient build and breakdown structured perfectly on phrases — the model DJ-friendly arrangement.

tracks.title: Spastik
tracks.why: A masterclass in slow additive arrangement and stripped intros/outros built for mixing.

title: Mixing Your Own Track
skill: Mix your track with EQ, compression, sidechain and stereo space so every element sits clearly.
content:
Mixing is making room

A great arrangement can sound terrible if everything fights for the same space. Mixing is the craft of giving each element its own slot in frequency, time, volume and stereo width so the whole thing reads clearly and loud. Start by setting a static balance with just the faders before you touch a single plugin.

Carve frequencies with EQ

Every sound owns a frequency range; your job is to stop overlaps. The golden moves:

  • High-pass everything that isn't kick or bass. Roll off below 100-300 Hz on pads, leads, hats and vocals to clear the low end — this single move cleans up most muddy mixes.
  • Cut, don't boost, to fix problems. If two sounds clash, dip one where the other lives. Subtractive EQ is cleaner than piling on boosts.
  • Carve a pocket: if the vocal and the lead both sit at 2-3 kHz, dip the lead there so the vocal sits in the hole.
ElementFrequency homeEQ move
Kick50-100 Hz + 2-5 kHz clickOwn the sub; let it breathe
Bass60-250 HzHPF below 40; dip where kick lives
Vocal/lead200 Hz-8 kHzHPF below 150; presence at 3-5 kHz
Hats/cymbals8-16 kHzHPF hard below 500 Hz

Control dynamics with compression

Compression evens out level so a part sits consistently in the mix. Tame an erratic vocal or bass with a 3:1 to 4:1 ratio, medium attack, and 3-6 dB of gain reduction. Use a faster attack to control transients, a slower attack to let punch through. Don't compress everything reflexively — only what genuinely jumps around. Sidechain (lesson 3) is your rhythmic compression: duck pads and bass to the kick so the groove pumps and the kick always punches through.

Reference at matched loudness. Louder always sounds better, so your compression and EQ choices will be biased unless you A/B at the same volume. Use a reference track turned down to your mix's level and compare honestly. Mix at a low monitoring level (you should be able to talk over it) to catch balance problems your ears miss when it's loud.

Stereo space

Width is the third dimension. Keep the foundation — kick, sub bass, lead vocal, snare — in mono and centered. Spread the supporting cast outward: pan percussion, stereo-widen pads and backing vocals, and place call-and-response elements left and right. Use a stereo imager but always check mono compatibility, because a wide mix that collapses on a mono club sub is a broken mix.

Depth with reverb and delay

Volume puts a sound forward or back, but reverb and delay set how far away it feels. Use sends (lesson 1): a short room reverb to glue drums, a long hall for the lead in the breakdown, a 1/4-note delay on vocal tails. Keep the kick and bass dry — reverb on the low end is mud. Less is more; a little space goes a long way.

Bus and balance

Group related tracks (all drums, all synths) to buses and process them together — a touch of bus compression glues a group. Leave 6 dB of headroom on your master so the mastering stage has room. A finished mix should sound balanced, clear and punchy at -6 dBFS peaks with nothing clipping.

Check on three systems. Big monitors, cheap earbuds, and your phone speaker. A mix that translates everywhere is a real mix; one that only works on your studio monitors is a trap.
exercise: Mix your track to clarity with the static-balance-first method. Set levels with faders only, then high-pass every non-bass element, carve EQ pockets where parts clash, sidechain pads and bass to the kick, and keep your low end mono and centered. A/B against a commercial reference at matched volume and on your phone speaker to confirm it translates.

tracks.title: Innerbloom
tracks.why: A spacious, beautifully balanced mix — study the depth, width and how clearly every element sits.

tracks.title: Losing It
tracks.why: A loud, punchy, ruthlessly clean club mix where kick, bass and vocal each own their space.

title: Mastering & Loudness for Clubs and Streaming
skill: Master your track to competitive, clean loudness that translates to club systems and streaming platforms.
content:
What mastering actually does

Mastering is the final polish on the stereo mix: a touch of corrective EQ, glue compression, and a limiter to bring the track up to competitive loudness — all while keeping it clean and translatable. It is not a rescue mission. A weak mix masters into a loud weak mix. Get the mix right first (leave 6 dB of headroom), then master.

The master chain, in order

  1. Corrective EQ — gentle, broad moves only. A 1 dB high-shelf for air, a small dip if the low-mids are boxy. If you need more than 2-3 dB anywhere, fix the mix instead.
  2. Glue compressor — 1.5:1 to 2:1 ratio, slow attack, 1-2 dB of gain reduction. Just enough to make the elements move together.
  3. Saturation (optional) — subtle harmonic warmth adds perceived loudness without raising the peak.
  4. Limiter — the loudness engine. Pull the threshold down until you hit your target, ceiling at -1.0 dBTP.

Understanding LUFS and true peak

Loudness is measured in LUFS (integrated loudness over the whole track), not peak level. True peak (dBTP) measures inter-sample peaks that can clip on conversion. These are the two numbers that matter:

DestinationTarget integrated LUFSTrue peak ceiling
Spotify / Apple / YouTube-14 LUFS (they normalize to this)-1.0 dBTP
Club / DJ play (WAV)-7 to -9 LUFS, loud and punchy-0.3 to -1.0 dBTP
SoundCloud / Beatport-8 to -10 LUFS-1.0 dBTP
Don't chase the loudness war. Streaming platforms turn everything down to -14 LUFS anyway, so a track crushed to -6 LUFS just sounds more squashed and lifeless than a -9 LUFS master that's allowed to breathe — and they end up the same volume on Spotify. Aim for punch and dynamics, not raw peak loudness. For the club WAV you can go louder because there's no normalization, but never at the cost of a dead, distorted master.

How loud is too loud

Watch the limiter's gain-reduction meter. Occasional peaks of 3-4 dB of reduction are fine; constant 6+ dB means you're crushing the life out of it — back off the threshold. If the kick stops punching and the track sounds flat and fatiguing, you've gone too far. The drop should still feel more powerful than the breakdown after mastering; if everything is the same loudness, you killed the dynamics.

Check the low end and mono

On a club system the sub is brutal and mono. Confirm in mono that the kick and bass still slam, and use a spectrum analyzer to make sure there's no runaway sub buildup below 30 Hz (high-pass the master at 25-30 Hz to remove inaudible rumble that just eats headroom).

Export and verify

  • Export a 24-bit WAV at your project sample rate for distribution and DJ use; let the distributor make the lossy versions.
  • Export a separate louder club WAV if you DJ it yourself.
  • Sleep on it. Master, then listen the next day on fresh ears and on multiple systems before you commit.
Reference, reference, reference. Load a professionally mastered track of the same genre into your DAW, loudness-match it to your master with a LUFS meter, and A/B. Your ear will instantly tell you if your low end, brightness or loudness is off.
exercise: Master your mixed track to a club and a streaming target. Build a chain of gentle EQ, light glue compression, and a limiter with the ceiling at -1.0 dBTP, then bring the limiter down until you read about -9 LUFS integrated on a meter. A/B against a loudness-matched commercial reference, confirm the kick still punches in mono, and export a 24-bit WAV.

tracks.title: Reflection
tracks.why: A loud yet dynamic club master — study how it stays punchy without sounding crushed.

tracks.title: You & Me (Flume Remix)
tracks.why: A clean, modern master that translates from earbuds to festival rigs — a reference for loudness done right.

title: Finishing Tracks, Sample Packs, Demos & Releasing
skill: Finish tracks and turn them into sample packs and demos you can send out and release.
content:
Finishing is a skill, not a feeling

Most producers have a hundred unfinished loops and zero released tracks. The bottleneck is never talent; it's the inability to call something done. Finishing is a discipline you practice deliberately, and it's the only thing that turns you from a hobbyist into a releasing artist.

How to actually finish

  • Set a deadline and a scope. Decide the track is done at the arrangement stage, not after endless tweaking. "One more change" is how tracks die.
  • Use the 80% rule. A finished, released track beats a perfect track that never ships. Your tenth release will be better than agonizing over your first.
  • Take breaks and return with fresh ears. Bounce it, listen the next day, fix the two things that actually bother you, then stop.
  • Get one trusted second opinion — a friend, a producer group — but don't crowdsource it to death.
Gig-test before you release. Drop your finished track into a real set or a recorded mix among professional records. You'll instantly hear if the levels, low end or arrangement don't hold up next to commercial releases — far more revealing than soloing it in the studio.

Turning a project into a sample pack

Your finished sessions are full of sellable assets. A sample pack is a product you can make from work you've already done:

  1. Bounce stems and one-shots — kicks, snares, your custom synth hits, vocal chops, loops.
  2. Key and tempo label everything — "Bassloop_124BPM_Am.wav". Buyers filter by this; it sells the pack.
  3. Make loops loopable — trim to exact bar lengths with no clicks at the loop point.
  4. Keep it royalty-clear — only include sounds you made or have license to redistribute.
  5. Organize into folders: Drums, Bass, Synths, FX, Loops, One-Shots.

Sell it via your own store, sample marketplaces, or as a value-add for your community (ties into the digital-products business path).

Preparing a demo for labels

DoDon't
Send a private streaming link (SoundCloud/Dropbox)Attach giant WAV files to a cold email
Research labels that fit your soundMass-blast 50 labels the same message
Short, personal, professional messageLong life story or desperate tone
Send your one best trackSend a folder of ten half-finished ideas
Follow up once, politely, after 2 weeksSpam follow-ups every two days

Release essentials

  • Master to spec (lesson 8) and export a 24-bit WAV — distributors and labels want the full-resolution file.
  • Metadata and artwork — title, artist name, genre, ISRC; clean square art at 3000x3000 px.
  • Pick your path: sign to a label (they handle distribution and promo, take a cut) or self-release via a distributor to Spotify, Beatport and the rest.
  • Register your work with a PRO/collection society so you collect royalties — this is real income (covered in the business path).
Ship consistently. One finished track every month for a year builds a catalog, a sound, and momentum. A single perfect track every three years builds nothing. Volume early is how you find your voice and how labels start to notice you.
